lectures.title: Sampling Distributions for Proportions
lectures.description: Establishes how sample proportions vary from sample to sample, detailing the parameters and statistics involved.

sessions.title: Parameters, Statistics, and Estimators
sessions.description: Distinguish between population parameters (unknown truths) and sample statistics (measurable estimators).
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this core lecture by establishing a clear, conceptual divide between the population and the sample. In a concept-first public lecture style, we want to bypass dry definitions and instead anchor our discussion in a compelling visual narrative. On the whiteboard, draw a massive, cloud-like circle labeled 'The Population (The Entire Sea of Data)' and a tiny bucket dipping into it labeled 'The Sample (Our Cup of Water)'. The core pedagogical goal here is to help students appreciate that in the real world, the population is an elusive giant; its true characteristics—what we call 'parameters'—are almost always unknown and unobservable due to constraints on time and resources. In contrast, the sample is tangible and measurable, giving rise to 'statistics' that we can actually calculate. By writing the parameter symbols (like $p$ and $\mu$) on the cloud, and the statistic symbols (like $\hat{p}$ and $\bar{x}$) on the bucket, we visually solidify the association: Parameters represent the Population, while Statistics represent the Sample.

To cement this logic, we transition to real-world scenarios, specifically analyzing polling reports. Suppose a headline reads, '62% of voters support the new environmental bond, according to a random survey of 1,000 residents.' We must lead the students through a critical mental process: Is this 62% the final truth of the entire population, or is it just the measurement from our bucket? Since it comes from the survey of 1,000 people, it is a sample statistic ($\hat{p} = 0.62$). The true parameter ($p$), the actual proportion of all registered voters who support the bond, remains hidden. A classic student pitfall here is confusing the notation or mistakenly believing that the statistic *is* the parameter. We proactively address this by emphasizing that statistics vary from sample to sample, whereas the parameter is a fixed, albeit unknown, constant.

Next, we introduce the concept of an estimator, linking it directly to the property of being 'unbiased.' Think of a target-shooting analogy on the whiteboard: if our statistic behaves like a series of darts thrown at a bullseye, an unbiased estimator is one where, on average, the darts center perfectly on the target. We show that if we take hundreds of random samples, calculate their statistics, and find that the mean of this collection of statistics equals the true population parameter, our estimator is unbiased. We present this not as a dry formula, but as a comforting statistical guarantee—the estimator doesn't systematically overestimate or underestimate the truth. This naturally prepares students for the next session, where we will explore how these individual sample statistics fluctuate around that center.

tasks: Identify parameters and statistics in specified polling reports.
Define the property of an unbiased estimator using sample distributions.

sessions.title: Sampling Variability
sessions.description: Visualize how different samples generate different statistics, forming the foundation of sampling distributions.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin this session by drawing a large, mysterious container on the whiteboard filled with thousands of red and blue marbles. State that the true proportion of red marbles is some unknown parameter, say, exactly 60%. Ask the students a fundamental question: 'If we take a random sample of 10 marbles and calculate the proportion of red ones, will we get exactly 0.60?' Some students might say yes, but most will realize that we might get 5 red marbles (0.50), 7 red marbles (0.70), or even 4 red marbles (0.40). Explain that this is not because we made a mistake in our sampling process; rather, it is the natural consequence of random selection. This introduces the core concept of sampling variability: the value of a statistic varies from sample to sample.

To visualize this dynamically, draw a horizontal axis at the bottom of the whiteboard labeled 'Sample Proportion of Red Marbles (p-hat)'. Simulate drawing a sample of 10 marbles, calculating the statistic (e.g., 0.50), and placing a physical dot on the axis at 0.50. Now, pretend to throw the marbles back, shake the container, and draw a second sample of 10. This time, we get 0.70. Place another dot at 0.70. Repeat this hypothetical process dozens of times, stacking the dots to build a dotplot. This visual pileup of dots represents the birth of a sampling distribution. Emphasize that each dot represents a summary of an entire sample, not an individual observation. A common trap for students is confusing the distribution of a single sample with the distribution of the sample statistics over many samples. Address this directly by pointing out that the elements inside our marble sample are individual colors, but the dots on our axis are numerical proportions.

Next, introduce the critical relationship between sample size and sampling variability. Draw a second horizontal axis directly below the first one, using the exact same scale. Ask the class: 'What happens if we increase our sample size from 10 to 100?' Simulate drawing a sample of 100 marbles. Intuitively, students will understand that with 100 marbles, it is incredibly unlikely to get only 20% red marbles if the true rate is 60%. The law of large numbers begins to show its strength. On this second axis, draw a pile of dots that is highly concentrated and tightly packed around 0.60, with very narrow tails. Contrast this with the first axis ($n=10$), which will be much wider and more spread out.

Use this side-by-side comparison to deliver the big conceptual takeaway: larger sample sizes produce statistics that are more precise and cluster closer to the true population parameter. This means that increasing $n$ decreases the spread of the sampling distribution. Warn students against another common misconception: the belief that the size of the population affects this spread. Clarify that as long as the population is much larger than the sample, only the sample size itself dictates the variability of the statistic. Conclude the session with a reflective challenge, asking students to describe this behavior in their own words or explain why a poll of 1,000 voters is fundamentally more reliable than a poll of 100 voters, laying the conceptual groundwork for standard error formulas in the next session.

tasks: Explain the concept of sampling variability in your own words.
Demonstrate how increasing sample size affects the spread of a sampling distribution.

sessions.title: Sampling Distributions of Sample Proportions
sessions.description: Establish the mean, standard deviation, and normal condition criteria for the sampling distribution of p-hat.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by transitioning from the conceptual nature of sampling distributions to their formal mathematical properties when dealing with sample proportions (p-hat). We establish that while any individual sample proportion is a random variable that varies from sample to sample, the distribution of all possible sample proportions behaves in a highly predictable way under certain conditions. The primary goal is to derive the mean and standard deviation of this distribution and establish the criteria under which we can model it with a Normal curve.

First, we draw a visual hierarchy on the whiteboard. We place the true population proportion (p) at the center of our canvas. We explain that the mean of our sampling distribution of p-hat is exactly equal to the population proportion (p). This proves mathematically that the sample proportion is an unbiased estimator. If we repeatedly sample from the population, the average of those sample proportions will center perfectly on the truth. We address a common student pitfall here: confusing the sample size (n) with the number of samples taken. Students often mistakenly believe that the mean of the sampling distribution changes if we take more samples, whereas the mean remains anchored strictly to the population parameter 'p' regardless of sample size or repetition count.

Next, we write the formula for the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of p-hat: the square root of p(1-p)/n. We write this clearly on the board and guide the students through its mechanics. By looking at 'n' in the denominator, students can visually grasp that as our sample size increases, the standard deviation decreases, resulting in a tighter, more precise distribution. However, we introduce a crucial caveat: this formula is only valid when the population is at least 10 times larger than the sample size (the 10% condition). We explain the physical intuition behind this assumption; if we sample without replacement from a finite population, the trials are not strictly independent, but keeping the sample size below 10% of the population makes the dependency negligible, justifying our use of the standard deviation formula.

We then transition to the Large Counts condition to justify using the Normal approximation. On the board, we write the two inequalities: n*p >= 10 and n*(1-p) >= 10. We explain that we need to expect at least 10 successes and 10 failures in our sample before we can safely map this distribution onto a continuous, symmetric Normal curve. If either value is too small, the distribution will be skewed (highly right-skewed if p is very small, or left-skewed if p is very close to 1). We sketch a skewed distribution side-by-side with a perfectly symmetric Normal curve to visually illustrate why the math breaks down without this condition.

To consolidate this understanding, we run through a practice scenario where we sample 100 students from a large university where 30% of students study STEM. We ask students to first check the conditions: Is the population of students at least 1,000? (Yes, satisfying the 10% condition). Are the expected successes and failures at least 10? (100 * 0.3 = 30, and 100 * 0.7 = 70; both are greater than 10, satisfying the Large Counts condition). Finally, we have them compute the mean (0.3) and the standard deviation (the square root of 0.3 * 0.7 / 100, which is approximately 0.0458). By completing this step-by-step verification, students bridge the gap between abstract mathematical formulas and practical application, readying them for formal inference.

tasks: Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a sample proportion given n and p.
Verify the 10% and Large Counts conditions to justify normality of the sample distribution.

lectures.title: Inference for One Proportion
lectures.description: Constructs the formal four-step process for confidence intervals and significance testing for a single population proportion.

sessions.title: Conditions for Inference
sessions.description: Review and justify the necessity of Random, 10%, and Large Counts conditions prior to performing calculations.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by establishing that statistical inference is not a set of mechanical calculations, but a rigorous logical argument. Before we construct a confidence interval or conduct a significance test, we must prove we have the legal mathematical right to do so. On the whiteboard, draw a bridge labeled 'Inference' spanning a chasm from 'Sample' to 'Population'. Explain that the three conditions—Random, Independence, and Normality—are the pillars holding up this bridge. If any pillar is broken, any conclusion we draw collapses. This framing shifts students away from viewing conditions as a tedious checklist and toward understanding them as essential mathematical safeguards.

Deep dive into the Randomness condition first. Explain that this is the absolute foundation for unbiased estimation. On the whiteboard, illustrate a target with a tight cluster of arrows far from the bullseye to represent selection bias. If a sample is not selected randomly, our sample statistic is likely biased, meaning its sampling distribution will not center on the true population parameter. Emphasize to students that no amount of advanced mathematics or massive sample size can rescue biased data. In AP-style questions, students must explicitly locate and quote where the prompt states 'random sample' or 'randomized experiment,' rather than just writing 'random.'

Next, introduce the 10% condition, which is often the most misunderstood. Explain the mathematical paradox: the formula for the standard error of a proportion assumes independent trials (sampling with replacement). However, in the real world, we almost always sample without replacement, which technically violates independence. Explain that as long as our sample size is small relative to the population—specifically, less than 10% of the entire population—the change in probability from trial to trial is so negligible that we can mathematically pretend the trials are independent. On the whiteboard, write the inequality $n \le 0.10N$ and explain that violating this condition actually means our standard error formula would overestimate the true variability, making our calculations inaccurate.

Transition to the Large Counts condition, which governs the shape of our sampling distribution. Draw two binomial distributions on the board: one where $n=15$ and $p=0.05$ (highly skewed right), and another where $n=100$ and $p=0.5$ (symmetric and bell-shaped). Use this visual to show that we need a large enough sample size relative to the probability of success to ensure the sampling distribution of our proportion is approximately normal. This normality is what allows us to use z-scores and normal probability tables. Teach students to explicitly show the products of $np$ and $n(1-p)$ (or $n\hat{p}$ and $n(1-\hat{p})$) and check that both are at least 10. Warn them against the common pitfall of saying 'the sample size is large, so the Central Limit Theorem applies'; for proportions, we must use the Large Counts condition, not the CLT, which applies to means.

Conclude the session with an interactive practice scenario on the whiteboard. Present a prompt: 'A researcher wants to estimate the proportion of defective microchips in a batch of 500. They test a random sample of 40 chips and find 3 defectives.' Guide the class to evaluate each condition systematically. Let them discover the trap: $40(3/40) = 3$, which is less than 10, meaning the Large Counts condition is violated. Discuss the real-world statistical consequences of this violation: because the sampling distribution is skewed, a standard z-interval will under-cover the true proportion, meaning our 95% confidence interval will not actually capture the true parameter 95% of the time. This leaves students with a profound respect for why we check assumptions before computing.

tasks: Evaluate a free-response style prompt to check if all conditions for inference are met.
Describe the statistical consequences of performing inference when assumptions are violated.

sessions.title: Confidence Intervals for a Population Proportion
sessions.description: Construct and interpret a one-proportion z-interval, including finding critical values and calculating the margin of error.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by transitioning from a single point estimate—our sample proportion, p-hat—to the concept of an interval estimate. The core intuition to establish on the whiteboard is that while p-hat is our single best guess for the true population proportion, it is almost certainly not exactly correct due to sampling variability. To build a reliable bridge, we introduce the formal skeleton of a confidence interval: Point Estimate plus or minus Margin of Error. On the board, draw a number line with p-hat in the center, extending arms outward in both directions to visually define the interval width as twice the margin of error. Emphasize that the goal is to capture the elusive, fixed population parameter, p, which remains stationary while our intervals shift from sample to sample.

Next, unpack the mathematical anatomy of the margin of error, which is the product of the critical value (z*) and the standard error of the sample proportion. Because the true population standard deviation of the sampling distribution relies on the unknown parameter p, we must substitute p-hat to calculate the standard error. Guide the students through this substitution, writing out the formula on the board clearly. Immediately follow this by deriving the critical value z* for a 95% confidence level. Instead of just handing them the value 1.96, draw a standard Normal curve, shade the middle 95%, and ask students what percentage is left in the tails. By visualizing the remaining 5% split into two equal tails of 2.5%, students understand that z* is simply the boundary line (the z-score) that traps the middle 95% of the probability density. This conceptual derivation prevents them from treating z* as a magical number and equips them to find critical values for any custom confidence level, such as 90% or 99%.

Now, pivot to a concrete application to anchor these formulas. Present a scenario where a random sample of 500 registered voters reveals that 270 plan to vote for a local ballot measure. Calculate the sample proportion (0.54) and walk through the step-by-step arithmetic to construct the 95% confidence interval. Watch out for a common arithmetic pitfall: students often forget to take the square root of the entire standard error fraction, or they round too early, leading to compounding errors. Write out every intermediate calculation step on the board—showing the standard error, then the margin of error, and finally the boundary values—to model the meticulous precision required on the AP exam.

Once the interval boundaries are established, address the most critical and frequently tested aspect of this topic: the precise interpretation of the confidence interval and the confidence level in context. This is where many students stumble by using probabilistic language incorrectly. Write down two distinct templates on the board to draw a clear line between them. First, interpret the interval: 'We are 95% confident that the interval from 0.496 to 0.584 captures the true proportion of all registered voters who plan to vote for the ballot measure.' Second, interpret the confidence level: 'If we were to select many random samples of size 500 and construct a 95% confidence interval from each, about 95% of the resulting intervals would capture the true population proportion.' 

Conclude the session with a practice prompt where students construct a 95% confidence interval from a new set of survey data. Use this exercise to check for two things: whether they correctly choose the critical value z* and whether their written interpretations avoid the classic fallacy of stating there is a '95% probability' that the parameter lies within their specific calculated interval. Explain to them that once the interval is calculated, the boundaries are fixed and the parameter is fixed; there is no longer any randomness, so the probability is either 0 or 1. Our confidence lies in the long-run performance of the estimation process itself.

tasks: Calculate a 95% confidence interval for a population proportion from survey data.
Write a precise interpretation of both the confidence interval and the confidence level in context.

sessions.title: Hypotheses and Significance Tests
sessions.description: Formulate null and alternative hypotheses, calculate test statistics, and determine p-values for a one-proportion z-test.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by establishing the core philosophical tension of significance testing on the physical whiteboard. Introduce the concept of the 'status quo' versus the 'burden of proof' using a tangible public-policy or consumer claim, such as a company claiming that 80% of their customers are satisfied, while a consumer group suspects the true proportion is lower. Frame the Null Hypothesis ($H_0$) as the world of no change, no effect, or the defendant's presumption of innocence in a trial. Contrast this with the Alternative Hypothesis ($H_a$), which represents the claim we are gathering evidence to support. Emphasize to the instructor that they must write these hypotheses on the board using the population parameter $p$, and immediately caution students against the classic pitfall of using the sample statistic $\hat{p}$ in their hypothesis statements. Explain that we already know the sample statistic; we are testing a claim about the unknown population.

Transition to the mathematical derivation of the test statistic by asking the class: 'If the null hypothesis is true, how unlikely is our sample outcome?' Draw a normal distribution curve on the whiteboard, representing the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ centered at the null value $p_0$. Derive the formula for the $z$-statistic step-by-step, showing it as a standardized distance: the observed value minus the expected value, divided by the standard error. Take care to highlight a subtle but crucial conceptual point: when calculating the standard error for a significance test, we use the null parameter $p_0$ rather than the sample proportion $\hat{p}$. Explain the logic behind this—since we are operating under the temporary assumption that the null hypothesis is true, our model of the sampling distribution's variability must reflect that assumed reality.

Now, define the $p$-value not as a dry formula, but as a conditional probability. Write on the board: $P(\text{obtaining a statistic this extreme or more extreme} \mid H_0 \text{ is true})$. Use the shaded regions on your normal curve sketch to visually represent this probability. Walk through the three possible directions of the alternative hypothesis: one-sided less-than, one-sided greater-than, and two-sided inequalities. Instructors should demonstrate how a two-sided test ($H_a: p \neq p_0$) splits the rejection region, requiring us to double the single-tail area to find the final $p$-value. This visual framing prevents the common mistake of forgetting to multiply by two when analyzing a two-tailed scenario.

Conclude the session with a collaborative practice scenario where students are given raw survey data—for instance, a sample where 42 out of 100 people support a new initiative, testing against a historical baseline of 50%. Guide the students through writing the formal hypotheses, checking that they use proper notation, and calculating the resulting $z$-statistic. Have them sketch their own normal curve, shade the appropriate tail area, and determine the $p$-value using the standard normal distribution. This practice is designed to solidify their mechanical execution while maintaining a strong conceptual grip on what the resulting decimal actually means before they move on to drawing formal real-world conclusions.

tasks: Write null and alternative hypotheses for a specified claim.
Calculate the z-statistic and p-value for a one-sample proportion test.

sessions.title: Interpreting Statistical Conclusions
sessions.description: Synthesize hypothesis tests by drawing conclusions relative to alpha significance levels, addressing Type I and Type II errors.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this final segment by establishing the absolute rule of statistical decision-making: the comparison between our calculated p-value and the predetermined significance level, alpha. The teacher should write a simple, visual scale on the board with alpha acting as the threshold. If the p-value falls below this line, we reject the null hypothesis; if it sits above, we fail to reject. It is critical to address the most persistent misconception in statistics here: we never 'accept' the null hypothesis, nor do we ever prove it true. The teacher should explain this using the analogy of a courtroom trial, where a defendant is found 'not guilty' rather than 'innocent' due to a lack of overwhelming evidence. By framing the null hypothesis as the default state of no effect, students understand that a high p-value simply means our data is not unusual enough to warrant abandoning that baseline assumption.

Next, we transition from the mathematical decision to the contextual interpretation. A formal conclusion must always bridge the gap between abstract numbers and the real-world scenario. The teacher should write a three-part template on the whiteboard: state the decision regarding the null hypothesis, state the justification using the p-value and alpha inequality, and conclude with a statement about the strength of evidence for the alternative hypothesis in the specific context of the problem. For example, if we are analyzing whether a new online learning tool increases the proportion of students passing a benchmark exam, the conclusion must explicitly reference the actual parameter—the true proportion of all students passing. This structure prevents students from writing vague summaries that lack statistical precision or omit the context entirely.

To deepen conceptual understanding and prepare students for advanced evaluation, we introduce the grid of truth: Type I and Type II errors. The teacher should draw a 2x2 matrix on the board, where the columns represent the actual state of nature (Null is true vs. Alternative is true) and the rows represent our statistical decision (Reject Null vs. Fail to Reject Null). We define a Type I error as rejecting a true null hypothesis (finding an effect that does not exist) and a Type II error as failing to reject a false null hypothesis (missing an effect that actually exists). The logical connection here is vital: the probability of a Type I error is exactly equal to our significance level alpha, while the probability of a Type II error, beta, is inversely related to the power of our test.

We then ground these abstract errors in a high-stakes clinical trial context to make their consequences concrete. Imagine a pharmaceutical company testing a new treatment where the null hypothesis states the drug's success rate is no better than the current standard of 40%. A Type I error would mean concluding the drug is superior when it actually is not, leading to the clinical consequence of distributing an ineffective drug to patients, potentially costing money and causing unnecessary side effects. Conversely, a Type II error would mean concluding the drug is not superior when it actually is highly effective, leading to the tragic consequence of abandoning a life-saving medication. The teacher should prompt the class to debate which error is worse in this scenario, illustrating that the 'seriousness' of an error depends entirely on the real-world context.

We close the session with an interactive diagnostic practice prompt. The teacher presents a scenario where a manufacturer claims that less than 5% of their medical devices are defective, but a random sample yield leads to a test statistic with a p-value of 0.082. Students are tasked with writing out the formal conclusion at a 5% significance level, identifying what a Type II error would look like in this exact scenario, and explaining its operational consequence. During this practice, the teacher should actively walk around to catch students who write 'the null is true' or who fail to state the alternative hypothesis in terms of population parameters. This exercise reveals whether students have truly internalized the connection between alpha, the p-value, and the real-world impact of statistical errors.

tasks: State a formal conclusion to a significance test in a complete contextual sentence.
Identify Type I and Type II errors and explain their real-world consequences in a clinical trial context.

lectures.title: Comparing Two Proportions
lectures.description: Extends the one-proportion framework to comparisons between two independent treatment groups or populations.

sessions.title: Sampling Distributions for Differences in Proportions
sessions.description: Derive the parameters, standard error, and shape characteristics of the sampling distribution of (p-hat_1 - p-hat_2).
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this lecture by shifting our focus from estimating a single population proportion to comparing two distinct, independent groups. To establish an intuitive foundation, draw two large, separate buckets on the whiteboard, labeled Population 1 and Population 2, with true success rates $p_1$ and $p_2$. Explain that in the real world, we rarely know these true parameters; instead, we take a random sample of size $n_1$ from the first bucket and $n_2$ from the second bucket, yielding sample proportions $\hat{p}_1$ and $\hat{p}_2$. The central question of this session is: if we repeatedly draw these pairs of samples and calculate the difference between their proportions ($\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$), what shape, center, and spread will this new collection of differences exhibit? By framing this as the creation of a third, synthetic distribution—the sampling distribution of the difference—we transition students from thinking about raw data to thinking about the behavior of a difference statistic.

Next, derive the center of this new distribution. On the whiteboard, write the expected value formula: $E(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) = E(\hat{p}_1) - E(\hat{p}_2)$. Since the sample proportion is an unbiased estimator of the population proportion, this simplifies directly to $p_1 - p_2$. Help students realize that this means, on average, the difference between our sample proportions will target the true difference between the population parameters. This is a highly intuitive result, but it serves as the stable anchor for our calculations.

Now, tackle the critical logical leap: the spread of the distribution. On the whiteboard, explicitly write the variance addition rule for independent random variables: $Var(X - Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y)$. This is a major friction point where students frequently make the mistake of subtracting variances. Address this misconception directly with a physical analogy: if you are guessing the length of two boards with some level of uncertainty, subtracting your two estimates does not make your final answer more precise; it makes it more uncertain. Because both estimates carry error, their errors compound. Therefore, we must add the variances of $\hat{p}_1$ and $\hat{p}_2$. Substitute the variance formula for a single proportion to show how we arrive at the standard error of the difference: the square root of $[p_1(1-p_1)/n_1 + p_2(1-p_2)/n_2]$. Emphasize that this mathematical derivation relies strictly on the assumption that the two samples are independent of one another, as well as the standard 10% rule for sampling without replacement.

Transition to the final characteristic of the distribution: its shape. Revisit the Large Counts Condition from the single-proportion model. For the sampling distribution of the difference to be approximately Normal, both individual sampling distributions must be approximately Normal. This means students must verify four separate conditions: $n_1p_1 \ge 10$, $n_1(1-p_1) \ge 10$, $n_2p_2 \ge 10$, and $n_2(1-p_2) \ge 10$. Draw two normal curves side-by-side on the board, showing that if both individual distributions are bell-shaped, their linear combination (the difference) will also be Normal. Warn students that failing to check all four conditions is a common point-loss area on the AP Exam.

Conclude the session with an interactive practice scenario. Present a hypothetical case where Store A has a customer satisfaction rate of 80% ($p_1 = 0.80$, $n_1 = 100$) and Store B has a satisfaction rate of 70% ($p_2 = 0.70$, $n_2 = 150$). Ask the students to verify the normality conditions for both stores first. Once verified, have them calculate the mean of the sampling distribution of the difference ($0.10$) and its standard deviation. This exercise allows students to practice the mechanics of the formula while reinforcing that the standard deviation represents the typical distance our observed sample difference will fall from the true difference of $10\%$. This sets up the logical bridge to confidence intervals and hypothesis tests in the next sessions.

tasks: Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution for the difference of two independent proportions.
Verify normality conditions for two-sample proportion comparisons.

sessions.title: Confidence Intervals for Two Proportions
sessions.description: Construct and interpret a two-proportion z-interval to estimate the difference between two population proportions.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by establishing the core conceptual shift from estimating a single population parameter to estimating the difference between two independent systems. Rather than asking what a single satisfaction rate is, we want to know how much better or worse one store is performing compared to another. Draw two distinct population bubbles on the whiteboard representing Store A and Store B, emphasizing that because we cannot observe the entire populations, we must rely on the difference between our sample statistics, p-hat_1 and p-hat_2. A critical pedagogical point to establish immediately is why we cannot simply build two independent confidence intervals and see if they overlap; doing so is overly conservative and mathematically incorrect because the variance of the difference of two independent random variables is the sum of their individual variances.

Next, guide the class through the construction of the two-proportion z-interval formula, anchoring it in the familiar template of 'point estimate plus or minus margin of error'. Write out the point estimate as the difference between sample proportions, and explain that the margin of error is the critical value z-star multiplied by the standard error. Take care to emphasize that because we do not know the true population proportions, we must use our sample statistics to estimate the standard error. On the whiteboard, clearly write the square root of the sum of the individual sample variances: the square root of [(p-hat_1 * (1 - p-hat_1) / n_1) + (p-hat_2 * (1 - p-hat_2) / n_2)]. Explicitly warn students that we do not pool our proportions here; pooling is a technique reserved only for hypothesis tests where we assume the null hypothesis of equality is true.

Now, transition to a practical whiteboard scenario. Present a dataset where Store A has 80 satisfied customers out of 100 sampled, and Store B has 84 satisfied customers out of 120 sampled. Before performing any calculations, demonstrate the mandatory habit of checking conditions. Write out the verification of the Large Counts condition for both groups, ensuring that the number of successes and failures in both samples are all at least 10. Once the normal approximation is justified, walk through the step-by-step arithmetic for a 90% confidence interval, mapping the critical value of z-star equal to 1.645 to the standard error calculation, resulting in a concrete interval.

Focus the next segment on the deep interpretation of this interval, which is where students most frequently struggle on free-response exams. Show how to write the formal interpretation: 'We are 90% confident that the true difference in the proportion of satisfied customers between Store A and Store B is between...' Then, direct the students' attention to whether the value of zero lies within the interval. Explain that if zero is included in the interval, it means a difference of zero is a plausible value, implying we do not have convincing evidence of a true difference in customer satisfaction between the two stores. If the interval is entirely positive or entirely negative, it provides strong evidence of a directional difference.

Conclude the lecture by addressing the classic interpretive trap regarding confidence level versus confidence interval. Ensure the teacher script clarifies that '90% confidence' does not mean there is a 90% probability that the true difference lies within this specific calculated interval. Instead, use a whiteboard visual of parallel stacked intervals to show that if we conducted this sampling process many times, approximately 90% of the resulting intervals would capture the true difference between the population proportions.

tasks: Build a 90% confidence interval for the difference in customer satisfaction rates between two stores.
Explain what a confidence interval containing zero suggests about the difference between the groups.

sessions.title: Significance Tests for Two Proportions
sessions.description: Perform two-proportion z-tests using pooled sample proportions for the standard error calculation.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by bridging the conceptual gap between confidence intervals and significance tests for two proportions. In confidence intervals, we did not assume the two population proportions were equal, which is why we estimated their standard error using individual sample proportions. In a significance test, however, our starting assumption (the null hypothesis) is that there is no difference between the two populations: $H_0: p_1 = p_2$. Because we assume these parameters are identical, we must treat our two independent samples as though they come from a single, shared population when estimating the standard deviation of our sampling distribution. This intuition introduces the concept of the 'pooled' or 'combined' proportion.

To make this intuitive on the whiteboard, draw two distinct sample buckets. Bucket 1 has a sample size of $n_1$ and $X_1$ successes; Bucket 2 has $n_2$ and $X_2$ successes. Draw an arrow from both buckets emptying into a single, massive 'pooled' bucket. This visual representation shows that the pooled proportion, $\hat{p}_c$, is calculated by adding the total successes and dividing by the total trials: $(X_1 + X_2) / (n_1 + n_2)$. A critical student pitfall to address here is the temptation to simply average the two sample proportions, $(\hat{p}_1 + \hat{p}_2) / 2$. Explain that this simple average is mathematically incorrect when sample sizes are unequal, as it fails to weight the larger sample more heavily. Pooling naturally handles this weighting.

Next, translate this pooled estimate into the standard error formula used for our test statistic. On the board, write out the standard error formula: $SE_{pooled} = \sqrt{\hat{p}_c(1-\hat{p}_c)(1/n_1 + 1/n_2)}$. Highlight how this formula differs from the unpooled version used in confidence intervals. This leads directly to the formulation of our test statistic: $z = (\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) / SE_{pooled}$. Emphasize that the $z$-statistic measures how many standard deviations our observed difference in sample proportions lies away from the hypothesized difference of zero.

Before diving into calculations, we must verify the normality conditions. Because we are operating under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true, we must use the pooled proportion $\hat{p}_c$ to check the Large Counts condition. Walk through the four required multiplications on the board: $n_1\hat{p}_c$, $n_1(1-\hat{p}_c)$, $n_2\hat{p}_c$, and $n_2(1-\hat{p}_c)$. All four values must be at least 10 to justify using the normal approximation. Warn students that using individual sample proportions for checking conditions during a significance test is a common AP exam mistake that can result in lost points.

To cement these concepts, guide the class through a full, step-by-step significance test comparing two demographic groups. Let Group A be $n_1 = 150$ with $X_1 = 90$ successes, and Group B be $n_2 = 200$ with $X_2 = 100$ successes. Have the class state the hypotheses, calculate the pooled proportion ($\hat{p}_c = 190/350 \approx 0.543$), verify the Large Counts condition, and calculate the standard error. Finally, compute the $z$-statistic and find the corresponding p-value. Conclude by interpreting the p-value in context, showing how a low p-value allows us to reject the null hypothesis and conclude that a statistically significant difference exists between the two demographic groups.

tasks: State the null hypothesis and calculate the pooled proportion for a two-sample z-test.
Complete a full significance test to compare the performance of two demographic groups.

lectures.title: Chi-Square Procedures
lectures.description: Explores non-parametric tests used to evaluate categorical structures across multiple distributions or classifications.

sessions.title: Two-Way Tables and Expected Counts
sessions.description: Set up two-way tables, calculate expected cell values, and compute the chi-square test statistic.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the lecture by drawing a blank 3x3 two-way contingency table on the whiteboard. Explain that this session serves as the entry point into analyzing categorical relationships, transitioning from simple percentages to structured categorical inference. Point out that while we easily observe raw frequencies (the "Observed" counts), the fundamental question of statistics is comparing what we actually see against what we would logically expect to see if there were no relationship or difference between our groups. Visually shade one cell of the matrix to highlight that every single joint frequency carries unique information.

Derive the formula for expected counts from the ground up, linking back to basic probability theory rather than presenting it as an arbitrary recipe. Recall for the students that if two events, A and B, are independent, then the probability of both occurring is the product of their individual probabilities: P(A and B) = P(A) times P(B). On the whiteboard, translate this probability model into counts: if we assume independence, the expected proportion of observations in a given cell is (Row Total / Grand Total) times (Column Total / Grand Total). Multiplying this joint probability by the Grand Total to find the expected number of physical observations yields the classic formula: (Row Total times Column Total) / Grand Total. This conceptual bridge demystifies the formula and ensures students see it as an elegant application of independence theory.

Next, guide the class through quantifying the discrepancy between what was observed (O) and what was expected (E). Ask students why we cannot simply sum the raw differences (O - E). Draw a simple matrix to demonstrate that these differences will always sum to zero, rendering a direct sum useless. Explain that squaring the differences, (O - E) squared, solves this issue and penalizes larger discrepancies more heavily. Then, introduce the crucial step of scaling: dividing by the expected value (E). Use a tangible contrast to make this intuitive: a discrepancy of 5 observations is massive if we only expected 2, but completely negligible if we expected 500. This division standardizes the discrepancy, establishing the single-cell raw contribution to the Chi-Square statistic.

Address a critical conceptual pitfall before moving to calculation practice: students frequently treat expected counts as if they must be whole numbers, rounding them prematurely to integers because "people can't be decimals." Explicitly warn against this. Explain that expected counts are theoretical averages over infinite repetitions, so they must retain their decimal precision (usually to two decimal places) to prevent rounding errors from corrupting the final test statistic.

Conclude with a collaborative whiteboard calculation using a 3x3 table representing consumer preferences (e.g., three age brackets versus three favorite streaming services). Choose a specific corner cell and have the class identify its corresponding row, column, and grand totals. Walk step-by-step through calculating that cell's expected count, showing the decimal value. Then, have students compute the raw contribution of this single cell to the overall Chi-Square statistic. This final practice moment is designed to solidify their mechanical precision while cementing the mathematical intuition behind standardized discrepancy.

tasks: Compute the expected count for a specific cell in a 3x3 contingency table.
Calculate the raw contribution of a single cell to the overall Chi-Square statistic.

sessions.title: Chi-Square Tests for Homogeneity
sessions.description: Perform homogeneity tests to evaluate if a single categorical variable has the same distribution across distinct populations.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by transitioning from the static mechanics of expected counts to the dynamic application of comparing distributions across multiple distinct populations. The word 'homogeneity' translates literally to 'sameness of kind.' Therefore, the core analytical goal here is to determine whether the distribution of a single categorical variable remains consistent across several independent groups. We establish this intuition by asking the class to imagine surveying students from three different schools about their preferred study environments—quiet library, bustling cafe, or collaborative study group. We are not looking at a single population with two variables; rather, we have multiple pre-determined populations (the three schools) and one categorical variable (study preference). This distinction is vital for avoiding the common pitfall of confusing homogeneity with tests of independence.

To formalize this investigation, we guide teachers to map out the hypotheses directly on the whiteboard. The null hypothesis ($H_0$) asserts a state of boring uniformity: the distribution of the categorical variable is identical across all populations. The alternative hypothesis ($H_a$) challenges this, claiming that the distribution of the categorical variable differs for at least one of these populations. Instructors should emphasize that $H_a$ does not mean every population is unique, but rather that there is some pattern-breaking discrepancy somewhere in the system. Before crunching any numbers, we must establish the gatekeepers of statistical inference: the conditions. We walk through verifying that data comes from independent random samples (one from each population), checking the $10\%$ condition if sampling without replacement, and ensuring that all expected cell counts are at least 5. We caution teachers to explicitly warn students that they must check the *expected* counts, not the observed counts, which is a frequent error on AP free-response questions.

Once the conditions are secured, we transition to calculating the degrees of freedom and determining the critical value. We show that the degrees of freedom for a two-way table is calculated as the product of the number of categories minus one and the number of groups minus one: $df = (r-1)(c-1)$. We sketch a skewed-right Chi-Square curve on the whiteboard, visualizing how the tail represents the rejection region. Instructors should walk through reading the Chi-Square distribution table, mapping the calculated test statistic and degrees of freedom to a bounding interval for the p-value. We explain the underlying logic: because the Chi-Square statistic sums the squared differences between observed and expected values, a larger statistic pulls us further into the tail, providing stronger evidence against the assumption of identical distributions.

To solidifying understanding, we introduce a classroom practice scenario comparing the distribution of primary transport methods (bus, car, walking) across three distinct high school campuses. Students will practice calculating the overall test statistic, finding the degrees of freedom, and locating the p-value. This practice moment is designed to reveal if students are correctly linking their final probability to a contextual conclusion. We guide teachers to model the phrasing of the final decision: we either reject the null or fail to reject the null at a specified significance level, and then write a complete conclusion stating whether or not we have sufficient evidence to claim that the distribution of transport methods differs across the campuses. We finish by reminding teachers to penalize active claims of the null (such as 'proving the distributions are identical'), reinforcing the conceptual nature of hypothesis testing.

tasks: Conduct a complete Chi-Square test for Homogeneity, checking all required conditions.
State the degrees of freedom and determine the critical value using a Chi-Square distribution table.

sessions.title: Chi-Square Tests for Independence
sessions.description: Conduct tests for independence to determine if there is an association between two categorical variables in a single population.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by distinguishing the Chi-Square Test for Independence from the Test for Homogeneity, addressing a classic point of confusion for AP Statistics students. While Homogeneity compares a single categorical variable across multiple independent populations (with fixed group sizes predetermined by the researcher), Independence examines a single sample drawn from a single population, classified by two separate categorical variables. To illustrate this, we draw a single large rectangle representing our total sample on the whiteboard, and then partition it horizontally and vertically to create a two-way contingency table. This visual metaphor helps learners see that we are not comparing groups we created; we are investigating whether two traits inherent to a single group are linked or independent.

Next, we introduce a concrete scenario: a market research firm sampling 400 random consumers to investigate whether there is an association between their preferred streaming platform (Netflix, Disney+, or Hulu) and their primary viewing device (Smart TV, Mobile, or Laptop). We guide the teacher to write the null and alternative hypotheses on the board, emphasizing that the null ($H_0$) always asserts 'no association' (independence), while the alternative ($H_a$) claims 'there is an association' (dependence). We warn teachers to caution students against using the word 'correlation' here, as that term is strictly reserved for quantitative linear relationships. Instead, they must use terms like 'associated' or 'independent' in their hypotheses.

We then walk through the raw data layout on the whiteboard, showing a 3x3 table. Students are prompted to verify the required assumptions: random sampling (given by the scenario), independent observations (using the 10% condition), and the large counts condition where all expected cell counts must be at least 5. We show how to calculate these expected counts under the assumption of independence ($Row Total \times Column Total / Grand Total$) and compare them to the observed counts. This process helps students see that expected counts are theoretical averages, whereas observed counts are the actual data collected.

To bridge the concept to statistical analysis, we display a simulated computer output of the Chi-Square test. We show how to read the output to find the degrees of freedom, calculated as $(r-1)(c-1) = (3-1)(3-1) = 4$, and the final calculated $\chi^2$ statistic. We walk through a practice exercise where the overall test is rejected (e.g., $p$-value $< 0.05$). The focus here is not just on rejecting the null, but on identifying *which* cells contributed most to this result. We teach students to analyze the 'residual component' or raw cell contributions $(Observed - Expected)^2 / Expected$ to pinpoint where the real-world behavior deviated most drastically from the independent model—for example, showing that far more laptop users prefer Netflix than would be expected by pure chance.

We wrap up by facilitating a reflective analysis. We ask students to explain in plain English what 'rejecting independence' means for the streaming platform's marketing strategy. This connects the abstract mathematical machinery of the Chi-Square distribution back to practical decision-making, cementing the concept-first, application-focused approach of this lecture.

tasks: Formulate hypotheses for a test of independence based on consumer habits data.
Analyze output showing a rejected independence test and identify which cells showed the largest discrepancy.

units.title: Inference for Quantitative Data
units.description: This unit covers statistical inference for numerical variables. It details sampling distributions of sample means, the Central Limit Theorem, and one-sample, paired, and two-sample t-procedures.

lectures.title: Sampling Distributions for Means
lectures.description: Builds the foundational mathematical behavior of sample averages, leading to the Central Limit Theorem.

sessions.title: Sampling Variability of Sample Means
sessions.description: Examine how sample means fluctuate around the true population mean, and calculate the mean and standard error of the sample mean.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin our journey into inference for quantitative variables by helping students visualize the leap from individual data points to sample statistics. Because the learner has expressed a preference for a concept-first, public-lecture style, we will introduce the concept of sampling variability not through sterile formulas, but through a thought experiment. Imagine a giant jar filled with millions of plastic chips, each printed with a number. The overall average value printed on these chips is the true population mean, denoted by the Greek letter mu. If we reach in and draw a single random sample of ten chips, the average of those ten chips, which we call x-bar, is highly unlikely to land exactly on mu. If we put them back and draw another sample of ten, we will get a different x-bar. This fundamental truth—that sample statistics fluctuate from sample to sample—is the core concept of sampling variability. On our physical or digital whiteboard, we can illustrate this by drawing a horizontal axis representing the value of x-bar, and stacking dots above it for each repeated sample we take. This builds a visual bridge to the concept of a sampling distribution, which is simply the distribution of all possible values of our sample statistic.

Now, we must address the mathematical characteristics of this distribution. First, we establish its center: the mean of all these sample means, symbolized by mu sub x-bar. Through intuitive logic, students can see that while individual samples will overshoot or undershoot the true population mean, the average of all possible sample averages must equal the original population mean. This makes x-bar an unbiased estimator of mu. Next, we turn to the spread of this distribution. If we sample only one chip at a time, our results are wild and highly variable. But if we average a group of chips together, the highs and lows tend to cancel each other out, squeezing our sample means closer to the center. This is why standard error—the standard deviation of the sampling distribution—is smaller than the population standard deviation. We present the formula: the standard error of x-bar equals the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size, n.

To prevent a common pitfall, we must emphasize the critical distinction between the population distribution, the sample distribution, and the sampling distribution. Students often confuse the sample standard deviation (from one group of observations) with the standard error of the mean (the variation across countless hypothetical samples). On the whiteboard, we can draw these side-by-side to highlight how the sampling distribution becomes incredibly narrow as n increases, whereas the population distribution remains static. This leads to a natural exploration of the mathematical relationship: because the sample size n lives under a square root in the denominator, quadrupling the sample size does not quarter the variability; instead, it halves it. This non-linear relationship is a frequent target on AP exams, and addressing it early builds deep quantitative intuition.

To solidify these concepts, we transition to an active thinking prompt. The teacher should present a scenario where a manufacturer knows their machine fills cereal boxes with a standard deviation of 1.2 ounces. First, ask the students to compute the standard error for a sample size of 9, and then compare it to the standard error when the sample size is increased to 36. By calculating 1.2 divided by 3 (which is 0.4) and then 1.2 divided by 6 (which is 0.2), students physically experience how a four-fold increase in sample size reduces the variability by exactly half. This exercise reveals whether students truly grasp the dampening effect of larger samples on sample fluctuation, cementing their conceptual foundation before we introduce the Central Limit Theorem.

tasks: Calculate the standard error of the mean for a specified population standard deviation and sample size.
Describe how the standard deviation of sample means changes as the sample size quadruples.

sessions.title: The Central Limit Theorem
sessions.description: Understand how the sampling distribution of sample means approaches normality as sample size increases, regardless of population shape.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by drawing a sharp contrast between the population distribution and the sampling distribution. The teacher should sketch a highly non-normal, heavily skewed distribution on the left side of the board—perhaps a right-skewed distribution representing household incomes or wait times. Explain to the students that if we draw individual samples ($n = 1$) from this population, our sample values will mirror this skewness. This sets the stage for the magic of the Central Limit Theorem (CLT): what happens when we increase our sample size to $n = 2$, $n = 10$, and finally $n = 30$? By visually stacking the sample means on a parallel axis below, students see the distribution of averages magically pull away from the skewed edges and gather into a symmetric, bell-shaped form. This visual progression is critical because it dismantles the common student misconception that 'as sample size increases, the population itself becomes normal.' We must explicitly state that the underlying population remains stubbornly skewed; it is only the behavior of the *sample means* ($ar{x}$) that transitions toward normality.

Next, we formally define the Central Limit Theorem. The core conceptual takeaway is that for any population distribution with a finite mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$, the sampling distribution of the sample mean $\u0004ar{x}$ will be approximately normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard error $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$, provided that the sample size $n$ is sufficiently large. The teacher should highlight the critical threshold of $n \geq 30$ on the board. This number is not a magic physical law, but a robust statistical rule of thumb where the skewness of most physical populations is sufficiently smoothed out. The teacher must clarify that if the original population is already normal, the sampling distribution of $\u0004ar{x}$ is perfectly normal for *any* sample size, even $n=2$. The CLT is specifically our bridge to normality when the population shape is unknown, bimodal, or heavily skewed.

To solidify this mathematical behavior, we transition into a concrete practice problem. Suppose we are looking at a highly skewed distribution of customer service call durations with a mean of $\mu = 12$ minutes and a standard deviation of $\sigma = 8$ minutes. If we take a random sample of $n = 40$ calls, can we compute the probability that the sample mean call duration exceeds 14 minutes? The teacher should guide the class through the logical checklist: First, is the population normal? No, it's heavily skewed. Second, is our sample size large enough to use the CLT? Yes, $n = 40 \geq 30$. This validates using a normal model. We then calculate the standard error: $\sigma_{\u0004ar{x}} = 8 / \sqrt{40} \approx 1.265$ minutes. 

We complete the calculation on the board by finding the z-score: $z = (14 - 12) / 1.265 \approx 1.58$. Drawing the normal curve, shading the upper tail, and finding the probability of approximately $0.057$ demonstrates how the CLT unlocks the power of normal probability calculations even for highly non-normal real-world scenarios. We close by warning students against the common pitfall of forgetting to divide by $\sqrt{n}$ when calculating the standard error, emphasizing that sample means are far less variable than individual observations.

tasks: Explain the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) and why it is critical when sampling from heavily skewed populations.
Apply CLT rules to calculate normal probabilities for sample means when n >= 30.

sessions.title: Conditions for Inference About Means
sessions.description: Review requirements for constructing t-procedures: Random, 10%, and Normal/Large Sample conditions.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing the crucial transition from mathematical theory to practical, real-world inference. Now that we understand sampling distributions, we must establish the protective guardrails that prevent statisticians from drawing invalid conclusions. These guardrails are the 'Conditions for Inference.' In a concept-first, public lecture style, we present these not as bureaucratic checkboxes to memorize, but as logical prerequisites that guarantee our mathematical models actually mirror reality.

First, we unpack the Randomization Condition. Why does randomness matter? Without random sampling or random assignment, our data is systematically biased, and the probability models we use to calculate p-values or confidence intervals collapse entirely. We explain to the audience that randomness ensures our sample is representative of the population, allowing us to generalize our findings. If the sample isn't random, no amount of advanced statistical calculation can rescue the analysis. We illustrate this by visualizing a biased net catching only fish near the shore, showing how it misrepresents the deeper ocean population.

Next, we transition to the 10% Condition, which represents independence in sampling without replacement. In the real world, we almost always sample without replacement. This technically changes the probability of selection for each subsequent subject. However, as long as our sample size, $n$, is less than 10% of the total population, $N$, the fluctuation in probability is so negligible that we can mathematically treat the trials as independent. We explain this using a simple jar of marbles: if we draw 5 marbles out of 10 without replacement, the probability changes dramatically; if we draw 5 out of 10,000, the probability barely budges. This condition is crucial because it justifies using our standard error formula.

Finally, we tackle the Normality Condition, specifically for means. When the sample size is large ($n \ge 30$), we can invoke the Central Limit Theorem to assume the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately Normal. But what happens when we have a small sample size ($n < 30$) and the population distribution is unknown? This is where students often panic. We guide them to understand that we must inspect the sample data itself. We use a whiteboard to sketch a sample boxplot, showing how to look for extreme skewness or outliers. If the boxplot is reasonably symmetric and contains no outliers, we can safely proceed under the assumption that the population distribution is close enough to Normal. We warn against the common pitfall of demanding 'perfect symmetry' from a small sample; instead, we look for 'no strong skewness' and 'no outliers' as our operational green light.

To consolidate this understanding, we run an active learning check where we present a hypothetical dataset of only 15 observations with a highly skewed boxplot containing a clear outlier. We ask the audience to evaluate whether we can proceed with a t-test. This exercise is designed to reveal the common misconception that the t-distribution is a magic wand that can fix any small sample. By analyzing this bad scenario, learners discover that violating the Normality condition on small samples makes our confidence levels and p-values unreliable, emphasizing the absolute necessity of checking these visual conditions before performing calculations.

tasks: Evaluate if a small sample size (n < 30) from a population of unknown shape can be used for inference using a sample boxplot.
State the assumptions necessary to run a t-test on a small dataset.
